name: Araucanian
confidence_why: The catalog's second-syllable rule rests on the four-page Echeverría & Contreras 1965 sketch alone, whose own recordings Echeverría 1964 had described as not phonemically predictable, while Lenz 1897, Zúñiga 2006, Sadowsky et al. 2013 and Molineaux 2014 and 2023 all put main stress at the right edge (final syllable if closed, otherwise the penult, with speaker and dialect variation in vowel-final disyllables), so the right-edge weight-sensitive reading is the probable answer even though the type of system is still argued over.
catalog_quote: Stress is generally on the second syllable. Secondary stresses on even-numbered syllables (Echeverria & Contreras 1965:134)

new_statements.quote: p. xxiv: "El acento tiene poca fuerza i poca estabilidad; a menudo cambia su lugar segun leyes poco fijas de equilibrio; por ejemplo: [scanned-garbled] mali ni súka (aquí está mi casa) pero: [...] Suká-mo kopán (de mi casa vengo)." p. 6: "el acento en jeneral en araucano no es fuerte, i fluctúa sobre diferentes sílabas de la palabra segun el ritmo del conjunto". p. 171 n. 320: "El acento en araucano no tiene lugar fijo ni en las palabras tomadas del castellano. He notado a menudo acentuación esdrújula por llana en tales palabras". p. 388 n. (1): "En jeneral se observa hasta hoi la regla establecida ya por el Padre Valdivia que las palabras araucanas se acentúan en la penúltima; solo cuando terminan en consonante suelen ser agudas".
new_statements.translation: p. xxiv: "Stress has little force and little stability; it often changes its place according to loosely fixed laws of equilibrium; for example: [famu] məli ñi rúka 'here is my house' but: ñi ruká-mo küpán 'I come from my house'." p. 6: "stress in Araucanian is in general not strong, and it fluctuates over different syllables of the word according to the rhythm of the whole". p. 171 n. 320: "Stress in Araucanian has no fixed place, not even in words borrowed from Spanish. I have often noticed antepenultimate stress in place of penultimate in such words". p. 388 n. (1): "In general the rule already established by Father Valdivia is observed to this day, that Araucanian words are stressed on the penultimate; only when they end in a consonant are they usually oxytone [final-stressed]".

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2, from Echeverría & Contreras 1965) counts from the left: primary stress on the second syllable, alternating stresses on 4th/6th (stress placement coded per word length as 01 010 0101 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable)). Lenz counts from the right: penultimate, or final when the word ends in a consonant, and says nothing about alternating secondaries. The two coincide only for vowel-final words of two or three syllables (both give σ2); for four-syllable vowel-final words Lenz gives σ3 vs catalog σ2 (+σ4), and for consonant-final words Lenz gives the final syllable (e.g. a 3-syllable C-final word: Lenz σ3, catalog σ2). Lenz also denies a fixed place for stress, which the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section; four scattered remarks. Lenz's positive rule (p. 388 n. 1, endorsing Valdivia 1606) is: words are stressed on the penultimate syllable, except that consonant-final words are usually stressed on the final syllable - a right-edge, closed-final-syllable-sensitive rule. He repeatedly qualifies it: stress is weak, has little stability, shifts its place by loosely fixed 'laws of equilibrium' and with the rhythm of the whole utterance (p. xxiv, p. 6), and in note 320 (p. 171) he even says stress 'has no fixed place'. Syllable prominence differences are small, 'as in many agglutinating languages', and stress moves when suffixes are added (p. 388).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on word-level secondary stress. On p. 388 (sung verse) he notes about half the syllables of a line carry 'a certain regular expiratory accent', the rhythm is mostly trochaic without excluding iambic, and one sometimes finds two adjacent stressed syllables or two to three unstressed in a row - a verse/phrase observation, not a word rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Consonant-final words are final-stressed (p. 388 n. 1). Spanish loans often take antepenultimate instead of penultimate stress (p. 171 n. 320). Stress shifts under suffixation and phrasal rhythm (rúka vs ruká-mo, p. xxiv; p. 388). In the transcriptions he marks stress only where it seemed strong or in an unusual position (p. 6), so the accent marks in his texts are not systematic.
new_statements.identity_note: Lenz's materials come from several dialects (picunche, moluche of central Araucanía, pehuenche, huilliche), and his stress remarks are framed for 'araucano' in general; the p. 171 note sits in Estudios V (Diálogos en dialecto pehuenche chileno), the p. 388 note in the Cantos (Estudios X), the p. xxiv/p. 6 remarks in the general Introducción. The Smeets record's open link actually points to a review of Smeets 2008 'A Grammar of Mapuche' (Mouton), not the 1989 thesis.

readall_conflicts: Lenz (1895-97) and the catalog's StressTyp2 record disagree in kind: the catalog's rule (from Echeverría & Contreras 1965, unopened here) is a left-edge syllable-counting rule with primary stress on the second syllable and alternating secondaries; Lenz states the traditional right-edge rule (penultimate; final if the word ends in a consonant) and says stress is weak, mobile, rhythm-driven and, in one note, 'has no fixed place'. The two agree only on 2-3-syllable vowel-final words. Lenz is internally tense too: 'no fixed place' (p. 171) vs 'in general the Valdivia rule is observed' (p. 388 n. 1). Neither of the two other listed works could be opened (Smeets 1989: the open link resolves to a 2009 review of the 2008 book and is bot-blocked; the Molineaux reassessment already held by the project from the compilation of 9/16 treats both as unreliable and argues for penultimate-mora / right-edge prominence with much variation, which sides with Lenz's placement rather than the catalog's. The standing conflict held by the project remains: the catalog codes Araucanian as strict fixed second-syllable stress with even-numbered secondaries (after Echeverria & Contreras 1965:134, unverified against a copy), while the sources already read (Lenz 1895-97, Echeverria 1964, Sadowsky et al. 2013, de Lacy 2014, Molineaux 2014/2021) are tagged as contradicting that coding (variable / morphologically and phrase-conditioned prominence, weak stress).

audit.recode_to: weight-sensitive, right-edge (non-strict): main stress on the final syllable if closed, otherwise the penult (right-aligned moraic trochee), CVCV disyllables variable; secondary/stem stress in a left-edge two-syllable window attracted by closed syllables. Sources: Zuniga 2006:63-64 (held), Sadowsky et al. 2013:94, Molineaux 2014:220, Molineaux 2018. Drop 'fixed-strict stress placement coded per word length as 01 010 0101 (1 = a stressed syllable) (E&C 1965 via StressTyp2), keeping E&C as a noted minority description.

sources.note: The article re-examines Mapudungun stress against the historical record of 1606-1916 and argues that the language went from weight-insensitive to decidedly weight-sensitive, with stress moving from marking the edge of verbal roots to marking the edge of stems, while right-alignment of prosodic units and left-headed feet stayed constant. Abstract only: the author manuscript on Edinburgh Pure sits behind an automated-access block, so no page-level quotation or check of the stress rules was possible.
